lessons.title: World Cup history
lessons.objective: You can name the eras of the World Cup.

payload.prompt: How many times has Brazil won the World Cup?

explanation.correct: Right. Brazil won five World Cups: 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002. Nobody else has more than two.
explanation.incorrect: Brazil has won five World Cups, more than any other nation: 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002.
explanation.sayThisLine: Brazil has five stars, that's the most World Cups ever.

pairs.definition: Brazil's first golden era; Pelé brought them three titles in 1958, 1962 and 1970.
Germany and Italy dominated; the tournament grew in reach and broadcast power.
France and Brazil's return: France won 1998 at home, Brazil bounced back to win 1994 in the USA.
Spain and Germany peaked; the last decade saw France (2018) and Argentina (2022) crowned.

distractorDefinitions: England won the first tournament in 1930 and remain unbeaten.
Italy won four titles and holds the second-most after Brazil.

payload.prompt: Which country did Maradona lead to a World Cup in 1986?

explanation.correct: Right. Maradona won the World Cup with Argentina in 1986, one of the greatest individual performances in World Cup history.
explanation.incorrect: Maradona led Argentina to the World Cup in 1986. He scored and set up goals; the final was memorable for his influence.
explanation.sayThisLine: Maradona took Argentina to the World Cup in 1986.

payload.statement: Pelé won three World Cups and remains the only player to achieve that feat.
payload.translation: Pelé won the World Cup three times: 1958, 1962 and 1970. He and one other player are the only ones to win three titles.
followUps: "Which team won 2022?" (Argentina; Messi finally got his World Cup.)
payload.noFakeExpertNote: Use this to join a debate about the GOAT without claiming to know everything.

lessons.title: The 2026 World Cup
lessons.objective: You can talk about the 48-team World Cup and its final.

payload.prompt: Who won the 2026 World Cup final?

options.text: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time
France beat Spain 2-1 in normal time

explanation.correct: Right. Spain won 1-0 after extra time, with Ferran Torres scoring in the 106th minute. It was the first World Cup with 48 teams, and Spain took it all.
explanation.incorrect: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time at the 2026 World Cup. Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute to give Spain the trophy.
explanation.sayThisLine: Torres in the 106th minute. Spain just won the whole thing.

payload.template: The 2026 tournament had {{teams}} teams split into {{groups}} groups of {{teams_per}}. The {{top}} teams from each group plus the {{best_third}} best third-placed teams reached the round of 32.

explanation.correct: Perfect. Twelve groups of four teams, with qualification decided by who finishes top two plus the eight best third-placed teams. That innovation meant third place could still qualify.
explanation.incorrect: Twelve groups of four: the top two and the eight best third-placed teams all reached the round of 32, so qualification was open to third-place finishers for the first time.

payload.prompt: What was new about the 2026 World Cup format?

options.text: It was held in the USA for the first time
It introduced a round-robin group stage

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 World Cup was the first with 48 teams instead of 32. This gave more nations a chance to qualify, though some worry about match quality diluting.
explanation.incorrect: For the first time, the World Cup had 48 teams (up from 32). The tournament was held across the USA, Canada and Mexico.
explanation.sayThisLine: Forty-eight teams at the World Cup, that's bigger than ever.

payload.statement: The 48-team format let more nations compete but some fans worry about dilution.
payload.translation: The expansion from 32 to 48 teams brought more smaller nations a shot at the World Cup, which is a fairness win but also meant more one-sided games in the group stage.
followUps: "Did the expansion work?" (Spain won impressively, so quality didn't suffer everywhere.)
"Who benefited most?" (Emerging nations, but also a few big sides that sneaked in.)
payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can share the complexity—more teams is fairer but riskier for match quality.

lessons.title: Ballon d'Or and GOAT
lessons.objective: You can discuss the individual-awards argument.

payload.prompt: The GOAT debate is mainly about...

options.text: Who scores the most goals in a year
How to weigh trophies, style, longevity and era
Who has the highest market value

explanation.correct: Right. The GOAT (Greatest Of All Time) debate hinges on what you value: does one World Cup count as much as longevity? Are individual brilliance and team success equally important? Messi vs Ronaldo vs Pelé vs Maradona—all have a case.
explanation.incorrect: The GOAT debate is about different measures of greatness: World Cups, Ballon d'Ors, longevity, era-adjusted impact, and style. Goals alone do not settle it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The GOAT debate is basically about what you value most.

explanation.correct: Right. France Football magazine awards the Ballon d'Or annually through a public vote involving journalists, coaches, players and fans.
explanation.incorrect: France Football magazine gives the Ballon d'Or. It's voted on by journalists, coaches, players and fans worldwide.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Ballon d'Or is France Football's award, the top individual prize.

payload.statement: The Ballon d'Or is often debated because voters have different ideas of greatness.
payload.translation: France Football magazine's Ballon d'Or is voted on by a worldwide electorate, and their choice often sparks debate about what makes a player the 'best' in a given year.
followUps: "Who do you think deserves it this year?" (Lets her voice an opinion.)
"Has your favourite player ever won?" (Gets her talking about her team's heroes.)
payload.noFakeExpertNote: Just know it's the top individual prize and there's always debate about who deserves it.

payload.title: The GOAT argument
payload.setting: She is defending her favourite in the GOAT debate.

exchanges.theirMessage: Messi's got to be the GOAT, right?

replies.text: He's got a case. World Cup, longevity, style—what do you weigh most?
replies.theirResponse: All of it, I guess. That's why it's so hard to choose.
replies.coachNote: Asks her thinking, shows it's complex.

replies.theirResponse: Fair, but Ronaldo's got something to say too.

replies.text: Pelé won three World Cups, he has to be.
replies.theirResponse: But he didn't play the same level of competition.
replies.coachNote: Dismisses her case with a fact.

payload.closingNote: The GOAT debate has no single answer; the fun is weighing different views.

lessons.title: Famous derbies
lessons.objective: You can explain the great derbies.

pairs.definition: Real Madrid vs Barcelona, Spain's fiercest rivalry. More than a hundred meetings, shaped by regional pride and a century of history.
Manchester United vs Manchester City, same city, vastly different histories. Recently heated by City's dominance and spending.
Arsenal vs Tottenham, neighbours separated by geography and trophy history. Both are gunning for the other's bragging rights.
Rangers vs Celtic, Glasgow's civil war. Scottish football's biggest match, with roots in religion and culture, always explosive.

distractorDefinitions: Bayern Munich vs Borussia Dortmund, one-sided for decades but Dortmund's resilience keeps it alive.
Juventus vs Inter Milan, Italy's biggest, but not a geographic derby—more a clash of eras and style.

payload.prompt: What makes a match a derby?

options.text: It's always between the top two teams in the league
It's a local rivalry with deep history and city pride

explanation.correct: Right. A derby is a local rivalry between teams from the same city or region, often with decades or centuries of history. Local pride matters as much as three points.
explanation.incorrect: A derby is a match between local rivals—teams from the same city or nearby. The history and local pride make it special, not just league position.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's not just three points, it's the derby.

payload.statement: In a derby, local pride matters as much as three points.
payload.translation: Derbies (local rivalries) are not just games—they're about bragging rights, city honour and a century of history. Fans often care more about beating their local rival than winning the league.
followUps: "What's the biggest derby in her city or country?" (Gets her talking about her own stakes.)
"Do derbies play differently?" (Yes—more fouls, intensity, emotion; sometimes sloppy but always fierce.)
payload.noFakeExpertNote: Ask which derby matters most to her team; it's always personal.

lessons.title: Bosman and the money era
lessons.objective: You can explain how the Bosman ruling changed transfers.

payload.prompt: The Bosman ruling (1995) changed transfers by allowing...

options.text: Clubs to demand higher fees from richer teams
Players to leave for free when their contract expired
Agents to negotiate for players without club permission

explanation.correct: Right. Bosman ruled that a player whose contract had ended could move to another club without a transfer fee. This flipped power to the players: they could walk away for free, forcing clubs to pay wages or lose them.
explanation.incorrect: The Bosman ruling let players move for free at contract expiry instead of being stuck with their club until it chose to sell them. It gave players power and sent wages and transfer fees soaring.
explanation.sayThisLine: Bosman changed everything, players finally had power.

payload.prompt: When did the Premier League begin?

explanation.correct: Right. The Premier League started in 1992 when England's top tier split from the Football League. It became a commercial global brand with massive TV deals.
explanation.incorrect: The Premier League began in 1992 as England's top flight. It transformed into a global commercial product with international TV rights.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Premier League turned football into a global TV product.

payload.statement: After Bosman, club wages and transfer fees exploded.
payload.translation: Bosman gave players leverage: if they were out of contract, clubs had to either pay them more or lose them for nothing. This sent wages up and gave rise to the modern multi-million-pound transfer market.
followUps: "How did Bosman affect the Premier League?" (England's wealth and global reach helped it become the richest league.)
"Is free agency good or bad?" (Good for player power, changes competition; fans debate endlessly.)
payload.noFakeExpertNote: It's a pivotal rule change; say it shifted power to players and changed football's economics.

lessons.title: Women's football
lessons.objective: You can tell the story of women's football and why the boom is recent.

payload.prompt: England's FA banned women's football on affiliated grounds from 1921 to...

explanation.correct: Right. The FA banned women's football for fifty years, from 1921 to 1971. When the ban lifted, women's football had to rebuild. The 1999 World Cup in the USA and the NWSL's 2013 launch then sparked a modern boom.
explanation.incorrect: The ban lasted fifty years (1921–1971). Even after it ended, growth was slow. Real momentum came with the 1999 World Cup and the NWSL's launch in 2013.
explanation.sayThisLine: The ban lasted fifty years and look at the crowds now.

payload.prompt: What event marked the start of modern women's football growth?

options.text: The 1999 World Cup in the USA

explanation.correct: Right. The 1999 World Cup in the USA (won by the USMNT) was a cultural turning point. Crowds, sponsorship and media coverage followed, leading to the NWSL's launch in 2013.
explanation.incorrect: The 1999 World Cup in the USA was a watershed moment for women's football. It showed the world there was appetite. Investment and media came next.
explanation.sayThisLine: The 1999 World Cup showed the world women's football could draw crowds.

payload.statement: Women's football grew slowly until the 1990s, then exploded.
payload.translation: The 1999 World Cup (USA) was a cultural turning point. The NWSL was founded in 2013. Investment, media coverage and participation have all surged in the last decade.
followUps: "Which team is she interested in?" (Gets her talking about the leagues and players she knows.)
"Why is it growing now?" (Investment, TV deals, player profiles, social media; it's now a genuine sport.)
payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can link women's growth to broader cultural shifts and media investment.

payload.title: Women's football is growing
payload.setting: She is excited about the growth of women's football.

exchanges.theirMessage: The crowds are massive now. So different from ten years ago.

replies.text: It's wild how fast it's changed. What's the biggest moment you remember?
replies.theirResponse: The 2022 Euros final. Fifty thousand people.
replies.coachNote: Shows you see the shift and asks for her memory.

replies.text: Women's football is the future, no doubt.
replies.theirResponse: I just like the game, regardless.
replies.coachNote: Overstate to sound supportive; she is talking about the sport, not politics.

payload.closingNote: She cares about the sport and the investment in it. Ask what she is excited to see next.

lessons.title: US soccer and the great seasons
lessons.objective: You can explain how soccer grew in the US and name benchmark seasons.

payload.prompt: Which of these marks a milestone in US soccer growth?

options.text: Pelé and the NASL in the 1970s
The 1994 World Cup hosted in the USA

explanation.correct: All three. Pelé in the 1970s raised the sport's profile. The 1994 World Cup showed America it could host and care about soccer. Beckham in 2007 brought global stardom and proved MLS could attract marquee talent.
explanation.incorrect: All three are milestones: Pelé drew crowds in the 1970s, the 1994 World Cup proved the appetite, and Beckham's arrival in 2007 showed MLS had arrived as a destination.
explanation.sayThisLine: MLS started in 1996 after the World Cup in the USA.

payload.prompt: What is the 'Invincibles' season in soccer?

options.text: Arsenal went unbeaten in the 2003–04 Premier League
Liverpool won five European Cups in a row

explanation.correct: Right. Arsenal went through the entire 2003–04 Premier League season unbeaten, earning the nickname 'The Invincibles'. It remains a landmark achievement.
explanation.incorrect: Arsenal's 2003–04 season where they did not lose a single league match is called 'The Invincibles'. That year is often cited as a benchmark of dominance.
explanation.sayThisLine: Unbeaten all season, that's the Invincibles.

payload.statement: Arsenal's Invincibles season and Manchester United's 1999 treble are benchmark achievements in soccer.
payload.translation: Arsenal went unbeaten in the 2003–04 Premier League ("The Invincibles"); Manchester United won the league, FA Cup and European Cup in 1999 ("the treble"). Both are held up as landmarks of greatness.
followUps: "What's your team's greatest season?" (Gets her talking about what matters to her.)
"Is winning style important?" (Fans debate—some love dominant seasons, some love ugly wins.)
payload.noFakeExpertNote: Use these as reference points for excellence, not as proof of which team is best.
